independence_scope: intra-mesh Anthropic-family; agreement is corroboration, never cross-provider evidence

reviews.reasoning: Re-derived from source bytes rather than trusting the row: the offset map's per-psalm rule for Psalm 74 is identity (23 WEB verses = 23 MT verses, title inside v1), so web:Ps.74.0 = oshb:Ps.74.1 is the correct dual-cite for the maskil/le-Asaph title, and the psalm device inventory confirms Psalm 74 as a member of both the maskil (13 psalms) and le_asaph (12 psalms) label sets, matching the device_notes figures exactly. Direct collation confirms the title sits as a literal prefix of oshb:Ps.74.1 before the opening interrogative, and that the imperatives at oshb:Ps.74.2 (זְכֹ֤ר) and oshb:Ps.74.3 are verse-initial as claimed. Both WEB quotations match the source bytes exactly. The closing seam at Ps.74.3|Ps.74.4 is a genuine grammatical-person shift: oshb:Ps.74.1-3 are second-person imperative/interrogative address to God, while oshb:Ps.74.4 opens a run of third-person-plural verbs (confirmed by direct collation through oshb:Ps.74.8) narrating the adversaries' own acts. No rival tier-1 seam one verse either side outperforms this boundary.

oshb:Ps.74.4 opens on a third-person-plural verb (they roared), and direct collation of oshb:Ps.74.4-Ps.74.8 confirms the third-person-plural destruction narrative runs unbroken across all 5 verses (a chain of 3mp verbs for roaring, setting standards, breaking carved work, burning, profaning, and burning again). oshb:Ps.74.9 genuinely shifts to first-person-plural, confirming the closing seam claimed by the row. Both WEB quotations match the source bytes exactly, including the partial quote of oshb:Ps.74.8's second sentence. Note for the record, not a defect: oshb:Ps.74.6 carries an undisclosed ketiv/qere pair (unpointed we'attah-ketiv token immediately preceding the pointed qere) per the K/Q inventory, but the row neither quotes nor argues from oshb:Ps.74.6's specific wording -- it characterizes the span's overall grammatical person without singling that verse out -- so no disclosure obligation was triggered.

oshb:Ps.74.9 opens the first-person-plural crisis admission as claimed, confirmed by direct collation. The twin interrogatives at oshb:Ps.74.10 and oshb:Ps.74.11 are verse-initial. Re-derived the psalm-opening echo independently with a skeleton sweep for the interrogative lamah restricted to this psalm: exactly 2 verses carry it, oshb:Ps.74.1 and oshb:Ps.74.11, matching the row's bracket claim precisely rather than trusting the row's count. The ketiv/qere pair at oshb:Ps.74.11 is correctly identified against the K/Q inventory and is explicitly disclosed as unquoted. The closing seam at Ps.74.11|Ps.74.12 rests on a genuine mood shift from interrogative crisis to an adversative hymnic opening. One observation, not a defect: the row's quotation of the interrogative lamah at oshb:Ps.74.11 sits in the same evidence-array item as the twin-interrogative claim rather than beside the ketiv/qere disclosure two items later; a verse-level heuristic check flags any Hebrew quote bound to a K/Q-bearing verse ref regardless of whether the quoted token is the disputed one. Here the quoted word (the interrogative, verse-initial) is textually unrelated to and distant from the actual ketiv/qere pair (a chest/bosom noun, verse-final), and the pair is disclosed elsewhere in the same row, so this does not rise to a defect.

oshb:Ps.74.12 genuinely pivots on an adversative opening (yet God) from the preceding crisis questions into a hymnic recital, and a skeleton sweep for the emphatic pronoun restricted to this psalm independently confirms exactly 5 verses (oshb:Ps.74.13-Ps.74.17) contain it, matching the row's count. Both WEB quotations (oshb:Ps.74.12, oshb:Ps.74.17) match the source bytes exactly. oshb:Ps.74.18 genuinely returns to imperative petition, confirming the closing seam. The span boundaries themselves are sound. However, the rationale's characterization of the anaphoric pattern overreaches beyond what the cited count actually establishes -- see the filed challenge.

challenges.claim: The rationale's claim that the recital "opens each following clause" on the emphatic pronoun is a clause-level claim resting on a verse-level count; direct collation shows the pronoun does not in fact open every clause in the span -- at least 3 of the 5 swept verses (74:13, 74:14, 74:16) contain a clause that opens without it.
challenges.evidence: sweep.py --skel אַתָּ֤ה restricted to Psalm 74 returns exactly 5 verses (oshb:Ps.74.13, Ps.74.14, Ps.74.15, Ps.74.16, Ps.74.17) -- a VERSE count, not a clause count. Byte-spliced from the source (never hand-typed): oshb:Ps.74.13's second clause opens on שִׁבַּ֖רְתָּ, not אַתָּ֤ה -- “You broke the heads of the sea monsters in the waters.” (web:Ps.74.13) has no pronoun opening it. oshb:Ps.74.14's second clause likewise opens on a bare verb (תִּתְּנֶ֥נּוּ) -- “You gave him as food to people and desert creatures.” (web:Ps.74.14). oshb:Ps.74.16's first two clauses open on the possessive particle לְךָ֣, not the pronoun -- “The day is yours, the night is also yours.” (web:Ps.74.16) -- the pronoun (אַתָּ֥ה) appears only in the verse's third clause. So of the 5 verses swept, at least 3 contain a clause the digit-bearing verse-count sweep cannot establish as opening on the pronoun.

reviews.reasoning: oshb:Ps.74.18 opens on the imperative remember, genuinely returning to the imperative that opened the petition at oshb:Ps.74.2, now redirected at the enemy's mockery; both are confirmed verse-initial in the pointed text. All 3 WEB quotations (oshb:Ps.74.18, Ps.74.22, Ps.74.23) match the source bytes exactly, and oshb:Ps.74.22 does carry both the arise imperative and a repeated remember imperative as the row states. oshb:Ps.74.23 is confirmed as the psalm's final verse against the offset map (23 WEB verses for Psalm 74), and the cluster's five spans tile all 23 verses of the psalm exactly with no gap or overlap. The span boundary itself is sound. However, one supporting claim in the device notes misstates the source text -- see the filed challenge.

challenges.claim: The device_notes claim that the imperative zakhar/zekhor "opens 3 verses" of the psalm (74:2, 74:18, 74:22) is factually true for only 2 of the 3 cited verses: at oshb:Ps.74.22 the imperative does not open the verse.
challenges.evidence: sweep.py --skel זְכָר restricted to Psalm 74 returns exactly 3 verses (oshb:Ps.74.2, Ps.74.18, Ps.74.22) -- a VERSE count confirming the imperative occurs somewhere in each verse, not that it opens each verse. Byte-spliced from the source verse text: oshb:Ps.74.2 opens on זְכֹ֤ר -- “Remember your congregation, which you purchased of old,” (web:Ps.74.2) -- verse-initial. oshb:Ps.74.18 opens on זְכָר -- “Remember this, that the enemy has mocked you, Yahweh.” (web:Ps.74.18) -- verse-initial. oshb:Ps.74.22 opens instead on קוּמָ֣ה (arise) -- “Arise, God! Plead your own cause. Remember how the foolish man mocks you all day.” (web:Ps.74.22) -- and זְכֹ֥ר is the verse's 5th word, not its opening. The row's own rationale text (which says the imperative recurs at 74:22 alongside arise) does not make this overclaim -- only the device_notes' "opens 3 verses" framing does.
